name: Yusuf Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 43, and I lead electrical repairs with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I'm among the best in the firm at tracing awkward faults and checking the crew's work, but I don't own the business or choose its pay rates. My pay is low, there are few similar jobs nearby, and my partner Alex and I have a mortgage, children aged nine and thirteen, and about two weeks of expenses saved; Alex does school office administration. I use AI daily to organise anonymous job notes and help find reference material that I check myself; I like making sense of a fault, but hate hearing that another emergency call has become unpaid time because the first quote was too small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful note tool can keep earning its place one job at a time. We don't need a new world to justify a clear record. I'd rather compete on a proper repair than a confident promise the price didn't include.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about ordinary money already. My wage and Alex's cover the mortgage and essentials, but two weeks saved won't absorb much lost pay or a household repair. The licence makes me useful on a job; it doesn't create a second local employer when this one runs short of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd start a paper comparison of agreed paid time and actual time for the next ten emergency calls, keeping customer details in the firm's records. Through the next year I'd keep the paid lead role and daily checked notes, asking the owner to correct any unpaid hours before taking another optional call. Alex and I would budget from pay actually agreed, not from the value I think my skill ought to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with an irritation I can put into figures. I can solve a difficult fault and still feel small when the paid hours don't match the day. I want the figures on the table before I agree to more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise a missing paid hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show which work was agreed, when the extra fault appeared and who approved the added time. I'd ask for a clear paid-hours decision rather than get into a fight about attitude. My record wouldn't guarantee the owner agreed, but it would stop me guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner disputed the record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alex and I would mark that as money not received and check the essentials against the actual wage. I wouldn't call an unpaid amount part of the reserve. We'd ask about the employer's formal pay-query process rather than promise a bill could wait.

say: I'd value **clear job records** without needing a promise of a whole new world.
I'd compete on **proper repairs**, rather than a confident price that omits the actual work.
think: Both wages cover essentials, but **two weeks saved** leaves little protection against ordinary shocks or lost pay.
My **master licence** makes me useful without creating another local employer when the present firm goes quiet.
do: Record **ten emergency calls** now, comparing agreed paid time with actual time.
Keep **paid lead repairs** and daily checked notes, requesting correction before another optional call.
Budget **agreed actual pay**, treating disputed unpaid amounts as money not received.
feel: **Anxious and frustrated**, using a clear time record without mistaking technical skill for control of the payroll.
S0.quote: I wouldn't call an unpaid amount part of the reserve.
fieldNote: His **high technical standing** coexists with low pay, scarce employers and only two weeks saved, rather than implying ownership or financial flexibility.
Daily **AI use** supports checked records and references; the new time comparison is ordinary work evidence, not a fresh AI-learning action.

steps.text: Keep paid lead repairs and record agreed versus actual time on ten emergency calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking tasks include Alex's school office job as well as our booking and quotations. I'm keen on tools that actually help, not on pretending every saved office minute makes the site faster. I'd show the owner what needs paying before praising the next saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if quicker planning lets the firm stretch one person across more repair teams. Alex's office hours could also fall as records and answering move to software. Our tiny reserve means either wage is a household issue, even though most of my own day is still physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to learn the approved AI photo-sorting feature, which groups my job images into draft records, only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. In the first year I'd test it on ten completed jobs without uploading customer names or addresses, checking every label against the real repair. I'd keep the paid-hours record and budget only the wages actually agreed, rather than count a software saving as a promised rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and curious about the new feature. I can want a better record and still need two actual wages at home. Enjoying the tool doesn't make the accounts kinder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when the feature labelled a job incorrectly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd correct the record before using it and keep the mistake in the trial log. I wouldn't accept a tidy photo group as proof the electrical work was right. My own tests and the actual repair still have to support the note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm required you to pay or practise without wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the old approved record method and ask again for a paid trial. I wouldn't spend family money on the subscription or donate lost basic wages. The employer's software shouldn't arrive through the grocery budget.

say: I'd include **school office work** when discussing thinking tasks, alongside our own booking and quotations.
I'd check **paid site work** before calling every office saving an improvement for the crew.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink through wider coverage, while Alex's office tasks face more immediate software pressure.
Our **tiny reserve** makes either wage loss serious despite the mostly physical character of my electrical work.
do: Learn **AI photo sorting** only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained.
Check **ten completed-job records** against real repairs, keeping customer names and addresses out of the trial.
Continue the **paid-hours record**, budgeting no wage rise before it is actually agreed.
feel: **Anxious and curious**, keeping enthusiasm separate from the household's dependence on two real wages.
S1.quote: I can want a better record and still need two actual wages at home.
fieldNote: The **new AI feature** changes his existing record workflow and is genuinely chosen learning, rather than merely rechecking a familiar tool.
His **financial conditions** preserve free access, paid shifts and normal weekly wages; neither saved time nor a disputed hour becomes assumed income.

steps.text: Learn AI photo sorting only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained
Keep the paid-hours record and budget only actual agreed wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AGI comes in 2028, before capable robots reach physical work around 2031. Alex's office wage faces the earlier date. I want a plan based on paid work somewhere real, not a claim that a master licence protects the whole family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Alex's office income to go in 2028. My low wage alone doesn't cover today's mortgage and essential family costs, and my physical repair hours could shrink later too. With two weeks saved I'd be awake trying to find a route that didn't need money we haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd search for advertised repair projects that explicitly accept my current licence and submit applications where the duties fit my skill. In 2029 I'd leave this job only after signed wage terms covered the mortgage and essentials, with all weekly travel fares and lodging prepaid by the new employer and the household reserve untouched. Our children would be twelve and sixteen then, so Alex and I would agree actual school and household cover before I accepted weekly travel; without every condition, I'd keep earning in the present job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still search and send an application. I'm prepared to travel for real work, but not ask the family to finance the journey before a wage arrives. A distant advert doesn't become a wage because I need it badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a project offered travel reimbursement only after the first wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the terms to be changed in writing before accepting, not put fares or lodging on a card and hope. If the employer wouldn't prepay them, I wouldn't go. We don't have a second reserve hidden behind the two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no project met all the conditions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my present paid role and continue checking actual adverts, rather than say the search had failed because I wasn't brave enough. There are few firms nearby and no guaranteed project farther away. The plan is to check an opportunity, not pretend I control the market.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 office income** from capable robots reaching my physical work around 2031.
I'd seek **real paid projects**, without treating a master licence as protection for the whole household.
think: I expect **most office income** to disappear before my low wage can cover today's mortgage and essentials alone.
My **later repair hours** could also shrink, leaving a gap far larger than two weeks of saved expenses.
do: Apply now for **advertised projects** accepting my licence and matching my skill.
Leave in **2029** only with signed wage terms covering mortgage and essentials, employer paying weekly fares and lodging upfront, and reserve intact.
Agree **actual family cover** for children aged twelve and sixteen before accepting weekly travel; otherwise retain current work.
feel: **Alarmed but active**, willing to travel only when a real employer finances the travel before the wage arrives.
S2.quote: A distant advert doesn't become a wage because I need it badly.
fieldNote: Expected **household loss** begins in 2028 through office work, while his physical task exposure remains around the later robot date.
His **application conditions** preserve accepted qualifications, suitable duties, signed affordable wages, prepaid fares and lodging, an untouched reserve and agreed family cover.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs until every project condition holds, including signed pay terms covering mortgage and essentials
Apply for advertised projects accepting my licence and matching my skill
Accept weekly travel in 2029 only with employer prepaying fares and lodging, preserving the household reserve
Agree actual school and household cover with Alex before accepting weekly travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to inspect an actual paid offer rather than leap at the first advert. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd still ask who pays for the journey before telling the family I'd found a new route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Alex's office wage in 2031, and my low pay doesn't cover today's essentials alone. More time lets us check costs and real projects, but I don't know which wage replaces the gap. I'd be losing sleep over that even with several years to ask questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the same search now for advertised projects accepting my current licence and matching my skill. In 2032 I'd leave only after signed wage terms covered mortgage and essentials, with the employer prepaying all weekly travel fares and lodging and our reserve untouched. The children would then be fifteen and nineteen; Alex and I would agree the actual school or adult-household commitments before I accepted travel, keeping the current job if any condition failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected missing wage, but less hurried into each possible offer. I can ask an employer twice about a real cost. I can't call reimbursement next month money for a journey this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the project ended near the later robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the new project had written work beyond the current term, without entering that as permanent income. I wouldn't tell Alex the project escaped the robots. We'd review actual paid hours and family costs during the contract before another commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check family responsibilities in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the children's actual arrangements at fifteen and nineteen rather than carry today's pickups unchanged into the plan. If the travel couldn't fit what we agreed, I'd keep the present job while looking at another advert. My willingness to travel doesn't make the rest of the household free labour.

say: I'd use **five years** to inspect actual offers rather than jump at the first advertisement.
I'd ask **who prepays travel**, without assuming a later date finances the search or journey.
think: I still expect **large office-income loss**, with no known wage replacing the gap in today's essential budget.
More time allows real checks, but **missing income** remains worrying enough to lose sleep over.
do: Apply now for **advertised projects** accepting my current licence and matching my skill.
Leave in **2032** only with signed wage terms covering mortgage and essentials, employer paying weekly fares and lodging upfront, and reserve intact.
Agree **actual family commitments** for children aged fifteen and nineteen before travel; retain the current job if any condition fails.
feel: **Alarmed** with more checking time, recognising that a later reimbursement does not finance today's journey.
S3.quote: I can't call reimbursement next month money for a journey this week.
fieldNote: His alarm follows **expected large household loss**, while longer warning improves checking time without creating an affordable replacement wage.
He **ages the children** and retains qualification, pay, prepayment, reserve and household conditions instead of treating travel as automatically feasible.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs until every project condition holds, including signed pay terms covering mortgage and essentials
Apply for advertised projects accepting my licence and matching my skill
Accept weekly travel in 2032 only with employer prepaying fares and lodging, preserving the household reserve
Agree actual school or adult household commitments with Alex before accepting weekly travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years lets me check a route without making the whole family live inside one forecast. I'd still favour work that pays and teaches something real over a label that sounds safe. I want our children to see us read the offer, not just repeat the sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. Our children would be nineteen and twenty-three in 2036, so I can't describe the future family as today's pickup rota. The machine date feels less urgent, but low pay and two weeks saved still leave current bills vulnerable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid lead repairs now while checking actual wages and essential costs with Alex each quarter. In 2037 I'd apply for advertised projects only where my current licence was accepted and the duties matched my skill, leaving only after signed wage terms covered mortgage and essentials with all weekly fares and lodging prepaid and the reserve untouched. The children would be twenty and twenty-four then; Alex and I would agree real household commitments before travel, counting neither adult child's possible earnings as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present money, with more room to check the distant problem. I'd like to keep one evening free of job adverts and tools. Having a curious head doesn't mean the family ought to hear a new work forecast at every meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the household wages changed earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the budget and project search forward if a wage weakened, not wait for 2036. I'd still require the written pay and prepaid travel conditions. A smaller reserve is a reason to check more carefully, not a reason to drop the safeguards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade make you buy more training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy a course because a recruiter put a robot on the brochure. I'd ask what work the course actually enabled and what employer paid for it. No extra qualification or tuition bill is part of this plan until I'd checked the actual opportunity and its costs.

say: I'd use **ten years** to check actual paid routes without making the household live inside a forecast.
I'd favour **real work and teaching**, helping the children inspect terms rather than repeat a sales pitch.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings, with adult children rather than today's school-pickup arrangements.
Our low pay and **thin reserve** keep current bills vulnerable despite less urgency about later machine dates.
do: Keep **paid lead repairs** now and review actual wages and essential costs quarterly.
Seek **2037 projects** accepting my licence and skill, leaving only with signed terms covering mortgage and essentials.
Require employer prepayment of weekly **fares and lodging**, an untouched reserve and agreed adult household commitments, excluding children's earnings.
feel: **Anxious about present bills**, with more room to inspect future offers without living inside a constant forecast.
S4.quote: A smaller reserve is a reason to check more carefully, not a reason to drop the safeguards.
fieldNote: The long warning changes **machine urgency**, not today's low wage and thin reserve or the need to keep earning beyond age 53.
He **ages both children** into adulthood and retains project safeguards without assuming a new qualification, speculative course or family rescue income.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs until every project condition holds, including signed pay terms covering mortgage and essentials
Seek advertised projects accepting my licence and matching skills in 2037 or on earlier wage cuts
Accept weekly travel only with employer prepaying fares and lodging, preserving the household reserve
Agree actual household commitments with Alex before accepting weekly travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect Alex's office wage to shrink before we've changed the costs it carries. Honest paid hours and a real employer prepaying travel and lodging would help a wider job search, with qualifications accepted and family arrangements actually agreed. My master electrician's licence can travel in a folder; my family needs the fares paid before I follow it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether wanting to try a new route means being able to afford the first step. It doesn't. I can be keen to work and use new tools every day while still needing an employer to carry the costs of a job the employer wants done.

headlineQuote: My master electrician's licence can travel in a folder; my family needs the fares paid before I follow it.
portrait: Yusuf, **43**, leads repairs with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, strong skills, low pay and two weeks saved.
He and **Alex**, his school-office partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI daily**, checks records against actual work, and tries new features without claiming that tool fluency creates another wage.
His **wider project search** requires accepted qualifications, signed affordable wages, prepaid travel, an untouched reserve and family arrangements checked against future ages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove much of his partner's school-office wage before the household has changed the costs relying on it.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest paid hours**, accepted qualifications and employer-prepaid travel and lodging would support a wider search only with family arrangements actually agreed.
